concepts.title: The Age of Revolution and the Birth of Sociology
concepts.definition: Sociology emerged in the nineteenth century as the child of revolution: the French Revolution upheaval in politics and the industrial transformation of work and city life posed problems no old framework could answer. The first sociologists set out to make sense of this new society -- its division of labour, its rationality, its classes and its despair.
concepts.key_idea: Sociology was born to explain the modern world at the moment the old order broke apart.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy204.txt lines 15-130 (introduction, sociology as child of the age of revolution, french revolution, industrial revolution and capitalism, enlightenment)
question_patterns: why is sociology called the child of the age of revolution
in class 11 introducing western sociologists: how did industrialisation create sociology's first questions
what problems of modern society interested the founders
connect the enlightenment with the birth of sociology
what does the term modernity mean in sociology
why were the founding thinkers European

solution_steps.explain: Nineteenth-century Europe saw political revolution, industrial capitalism and urban upheaval -- a society unlike anything before.
Factory discipline, class conflict, urban anonymity and scientific worldview demanded new concepts and methods.
Sociology arose to analyse this modernity, and its founding thinkers each took a different slice of it.

worked_examples.q: Sociology emerged as the child of revolution in which century?

concepts.title: Karl Marx: Classes, Capital and Conflict
concepts.definition: Marx read history as the history of class struggle. Under capitalism the two central classes are the bourgeoisie, owners of the means of production, and the proletariat, sellers of labour power. Surplus value extracted from workers drives accumulation and alienation -- workers estranged from their product, their work and themselves -- until, Marx predicted, the system's contradictions transform it.
concepts.key_idea: Who owns production decides who rules -- class struggle is the motor of history and alienation its human cost.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy204.txt lines 130-280 (karl marx, class struggle, bourgeoisie and proletariat, surplus value, alienation, materialist conception of history)
question_patterns: explain marx's idea of class struggle as the motor of history
in class 11 introducing western sociologists: what are surplus value and exploitation
describe the two main classes of capitalist society
what does alienation of labour mean
how does the materialist view of history differ from idealism
why did marx think capitalism carries the seeds of its own transformation

solution_steps.explain: Follow ownership: those who own factories and land (bourgeoisie) confront those who own only their labour (proletariat).
Workers produce more value than they are paid; the surplus accrues to owners -- the mechanism of exploitation.
Assembly-line work estranges workers from product, process and fellow workers -- alienation -- while class conflict drives historical change.

worked_examples.q: Marx read history as the history of what?

concepts.title: Emile Durkheim: Social Facts, Solidarity and Suicide
concepts.definition: Durkheim insisted society is a reality of its own: social facts -- norms, institutions, currents of opinion -- exist outside individuals and constrain them, and must be explained by other social facts. He traced the shift from mechanical solidarity (likeness-based, in simple societies) to organic solidarity (interdependence-based, in complex ones) and used suicide rates to show even the most personal act follows social currents.
concepts.key_idea: Society is a thing with its own forces -- even suicide rates follow social facts, not private moods.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy204.txt lines 280-420 (emile durkheim, social facts, mechanical and organic solidarity, division of labour, suicide as social, anomie)
question_patterns: what are social facts and how should they be studied
in class 11 introducing western sociologists: distinguish mechanical and organic solidarity
how does durkheim explain suicide as a social phenomenon
what is anomie and when does it arise
why did durkheim treat the division of labour as moral as well as economic
how does durkheim differ from marx on what holds society together

solution_steps.explain: Social facts are collective ways of acting and thinking external to individuals and coercive upon them.
Small homogeneous societies cohere by likeness (mechanical); large differentiated ones cohere by mutual dependence (organic).
Suicide rates vary with integration and regulation -- egoistic, altruistic and anomic types -- proving even intimate acts carry social causes.

worked_examples.q: Norms and institutions existing outside individuals and constraining them are called social what?

concepts.title: Max Weber: Rationalisation, Bureaucracy and the Protestant Ethic
concepts.definition: Weber saw modernity as rationalisation -- the relentless organisation of life around efficiency, calculation and rules. Its purest instrument is bureaucracy, hierarchy of offices with written rules and impersonal operation. Against materialism he argued ideas matter too: the Protestant ethic's inner-worldly discipline, he claimed, helped birth the spirit of capitalism.
concepts.key_idea: Modernity is the triumph of calculation -- bureaucratic rules everywhere, and even capitalism has a religious biography.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy204.txt lines 420-560 (max weber, rationalisation, bureaucracy, protestant ethic and spirit of capitalism, ideal types, understanding social action)
question_patterns: what does weber mean by rationalisation of society
in class 11 introducing western sociologists: describe the features of bureaucracy according to weber
how does the protestant ethic relate to the spirit of capitalism
why did weber fear the iron cage of rationality
distinguish weber's approach from marx's on the origin of capitalism
what are ideal types and why does weber use them

solution_steps.explain: Modernity replaces tradition and sentiment with calculated, rule-governed efficiency -- rationalisation in every sphere.
Bureaucracy -- offices, hierarchies, files, impersonality -- is rationalisation's most powerful embodiment, efficient yet entangling like an iron cage.
Weber's Protestant ethic study showed religiously rooted discipline and calling could feed capitalist accumulation -- ideas share causal work with economics.

worked_examples.q: Weber saw modernity as the relentless organisation of life around efficiency and rules, called what?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A garment worker stitches shirts all day in a factory but cannot afford one. Explain this case using surplus value and alienation.

solution_template.explain: The value she adds in a day far exceeds her wage; the difference is surplus, taken by the owner -- the exploitation mechanism.
Repeating one stitch-sequence, owning neither product nor process, she is estranged from the work and its fruit -- unable to buy the shirt she makes.
Her situation is not personal bad luck but her structural position in the class relation Marx analysed.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Suicide rates are found to be higher among uprooted migrants in a big city than among settled villagers. Interpret the finding using Durkheim's concepts.

solution_template.explain: Durkheim begins with the pattern in rates, not individual motives -- a social fact to be explained socially.
Migrants lack the dense ties and shared norms of village life -- weak integration and uncertain regulation mark egoistic and anomic types.
The gap in rates reflects differing social currents, confirming Durkheim's claim that even suicide follows society.
